title: A Strongly Subcubic Combinatorial Algorithm for Triangle Detection with Applications

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2, case analysis claiming that BFS+(s) finds a triangle whenever s is in the closed neighborhood of a triangle
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The central assertion is not established. In Case 2.1 the paper says that if only a is on BFS level 1, then b and c are on level 2 and, "assuming that b is discovered before c, the triangle {a,b,c} is detected while scanning the adjacency list of b." This does not follow: b and c need not have a as their BFS parent, and merely encountering the same-level edge bc does not identify a common neighbor and hence does not certify a triangle. For example, take vertices s,p,a,b,c and edges sa, sp, pb, ab, ac, bc. If p is processed before a, then b is discovered from p and c from a; the only triangle is abc, but b and c have different BFS parents. Detecting that a is a common neighbor of b and c requires an additional common-neighbor search not described in the proof. The analogous unproved issue occurs whenever multiple vertices on the previous BFS level are adjacent to level-two vertices.

predicted_errors.error_location: Definition and time analysis of BFS+ in Theorem 2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The algorithm BFS+ is never actually specified. The paper refers to a "slightly modified version of BFS," to "Step 12 of the modified BFS procedure," and bases the entire result on it, but no BFS+ pseudocode or Step 12 appears in the document. The time bound assumes each BFS+ call costs O(m), as for ordinary BFS. However, the omitted operation would have to determine whether endpoints of a same-level edge have an appropriate common neighbor; naively this is not an O(1) operation and can require examining many neighbor pairs. Thus the claimed O(m) per-trial cost, and consequently the O(m^(2/3)n), O(m sqrt(n)), and O(m^(4/3)) bounds, are unsupported by the described method.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 5, count of weight triples and union-bound calculation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states: "There are less than m^3 possible triples (z01,z12,z20) to consider." Each edge weight can be zero and can be as large as m, so each zij has up to m+1 possible values. The direct count is at most (m+1)^3, not less than m^3. Consequently the stated union-bound calculation m^3 · 10^-30 · m^-3 = 10^-30 does not establish the advertised failure probability at most 10^-30. This can be repaired by changing constants/error amplification, but it is incorrect as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, sentence claiming invalidation of the combinatorial k-clique conjecture "by a polynomial factor, n^(2k/9)"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The asserted factor is only the saving for k divisible by 3. Theorem 4 itself gives exponent (7k+2)/9 for k=3ℓ+1 and (7k+4)/9 for k=3ℓ+2. Relative to n^k, these are savings n^((2k-2)/9) and n^((2k-4)/9), respectively, not n^(2k/9). For example, k=4 gives runtime n^(10/3), a saving n^(2/3), whereas n^(2k/9)=n^(8/9). The unqualified statement is therefore quantitatively false.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract; statements following Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 claiming the first truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms for triangle detection and BMM
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: These conclusions depend entirely on the invalid/unimplemented BFS+ subroutine. The paper has not shown that a sampled neighbor of a triangle permits an O(m)-time BFS procedure to find that triangle, nor supplied an implementation with that complexity. Therefore Theorem 2 is unproved, and the claimed BMM consequence in Theorem 3, the k-clique results, Max-Cut result, and the broad claims of invalidating longstanding conjectures do not follow.
